claim: rDNA loci are composed of hundreds of tandemly duplicated arrays of rRNA genes.
source: rDNA loci, composed of hundreds of tandemly duplicated arrays of rRNA genes, are known to be among the most unstable genetic elements due to their repetitive nature.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of rDNA loci.

claim: rDNA loci are among the most unstable genetic elements due to their repetitive nature.
source: rDNA loci, composed of hundreds of tandemly duplicated arrays of rRNA genes, are known to be among the most unstable genetic elements due to their repetitive nature.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: rDNA instability underlies aging (replicative senescence) in yeast cells.
source: rDNA instability underlies aging (replicative senescence) in yeast cells, however, its contribution to the aging of multicellular organisms is poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: rDNA copy number decreases during aging in Drosophila male germline stem cells.
source: In this study, we investigate the dynamics of rDNA loci during aging in the Drosophila male germline stem cell (GSC) lineage, and show that rDNA copy number decreases during aging.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by qPCR and FISH data in the results.

claim: Age-dependent decrease in rDNA copy number is heritable from generation to generation.
source: Our study further reveals that this age-dependent decrease in rDNA copy number is heritable from generation to generation, yet GSCs in young animals that inherited reduced rDNA copy number are capable of recovering normal rDNA copy number.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: GSCs in young animals that inherited reduced rDNA copy number are capable of recovering normal rDNA copy number.
source: Our study further reveals that this age-dependent decrease in rDNA copy number is heritable from generation to generation, yet GSCs in young animals that inherited reduced rDNA copy number are capable of recovering normal rDNA copy number.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: rDNA can undergo intrachromatid recombination leading to copy number loss and generation of extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs).
source: First, as an inherent characteristic of repetitive DNA, rDNA can undergo intrachromatid recombination leading to copy number loss and generation of circularized repeat units (extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs)) (Figure 1A) (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The rDNA is highly transcribed even during S phase, leading to possible collisions between replication and transcription machineries.
source: Second, the rDNA is highly transcribed even during S phase, leading to possible collisions between replication and transcription machineries.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of rDNA in the introduction.

claim: Collision between replication and transcription machineries can result in double strand breaks, contributing to genomic instability of the rDNA.
source: This collision can result in double strand breaks, further contributing to genomic instability of the rDNA (Helmrich et al., 2013; Takeuchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster exhibits 6-fold range of rDNA copy number.
source: For example, it has been shown that Drosophila melanogaster exhibits 6-fold range of rDNA copy number (Lyckegaard and Clark, 1989; Lyckegaard and Clark, 1991), and another study estimated copy number range to be 80–600, where individuals with >130 copies are asymptomatic (Mohan and Ritossa, 1970).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior studies.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, rDNA copy number range is estimated to be 80–600, where individuals with >130 copies are asymptomatic.
source: For example, it has been shown that Drosophila melanogaster exhibits 6-fold range of rDNA copy number (Lyckegaard and Clark, 1989; Lyckegaard and Clark, 1991), and another study estimated copy number range to be 80–600, where individuals with >130 copies are asymptomatic (Mohan and Ritossa, 1970).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior study.

claim: rDNA copy number variation has been observed in many species including budding and fission yeasts, planktonic crustaceans Daphnia, plants, mouse and humans.
source: Similarly, rDNA copy number variation has been observed in many species including budding and fission yeasts (James et al., 2009; Maleszka and Clark-Walker, 1993; Pasero and Marilley, 1993), planktonic crustaceans Daphnia (Eagle and Crease, 2012), plants (barley [Zhang et al., 1990], bell bean [Rogers and Bendich, 1987]), mouse (Gibbons et al., 2015) and humans (Gibbons et al., 2015; Gibbons et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The range of rDNA copy number is well maintained within populations despite striking copy number variation among individuals.
source: Despite striking copy number variation among individuals, the range of copy number is well maintained within the population, suggestive of a mechanism that maintains rDNA copy number through generations.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the literature.

claim: In yeast, rDNA instability (reduction of rDNA copy number and associated accumulation of ERCs) is a major cause of replicative aging/senescence.
source: In yeast, rDNA instability (i.e. reduction of rDNA copy number and associated accumulation of ERCs) is a major cause of replicative aging/senescence (Ganley and Kobayashi, 2014; Kobayashi, 2011; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: The state of rDNA stability in various yeast mutants correlates well with lengthened or shortened life span.
source: The state of rDNA stability in various mutants that either stabilize or decrease rDNA copy number correlates well with lengthened or shortened life span, respectively (Ganley and Kobayashi, 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Stem cells proliferate throughout the life of multicellular organisms.
source: In particular, stem cells proliferate throughout the life of multicellular organisms, and their declining number and/or function during aging is proposed to be an underlying cause of organismal aging, due to inability to replenish essential cell populations (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Declining number and/or function of stem cells during aging is proposed to be an underlying cause of organismal aging.
source: In particular, stem cells proliferate throughout the life of multicellular organisms, and their declining number and/or function during aging is proposed to be an underlying cause of organismal aging, due to inability to replenish essential cell populations (López-Otín et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Drosophila male GSCs undergo continuous asymmetric divisions throughout adulthood, producing one self-renewed GSC and one differentiating cell.
source: GSCs undergo continuous asymmetric divisions throughout adulthood, producing one self-renewed GSC and one differentiating cell (Inaba and Yamashita, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Drosophila rDNA loci are limited to the sex chromosomes (X and Y).
source: Additionally, Drosophila rDNA loci are limited to the sex chromosomes (X and Y), providing a simplified system to assess rDNA stability compared to other animal models that have multiple rDNA loci spread across many chromosomes (McStay, 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Most GSCs in young males contain a single, round nucleolus approximately 2 μm in diameter (89.2%, n = 408).
source: Immunofluorescence staining of the nucleolar component Fibrillarin (Ochs et al., 1985) showed that most GSCs in young males contain a single, round nucleolus approximately 2 μm in diameter (89.2%, n = 408, Figure 1B, 'typical').
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The frequency of GSCs with typical nucleolar morphology progressively decreased during aging throughout 40 days of adulthood.
source: However, we found that the frequency of GSCs with typical nucleolar morphology progressively decreased during aging throughout 40 days of adulthood (Figure 1C), as the GSCs with atypical nucleolar morphology increased.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The nucleolus is organized by transcription of the rDNA.
source: The nucleolus is organized by transcription of the rDNA, thus its morphology is expected to reflect the transcriptional activity of rDNA loci (Boisvert et al., 2007; Pederson, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Nucleolar morphology reflects the transcriptional activity of rDNA loci.
source: The nucleolus is organized by transcription of the rDNA, thus its morphology is expected to reflect the transcriptional activity of rDNA loci (Boisvert et al., 2007; Pederson, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, the X and Y rDNA loci each contain ~200–250 copies of rDNA.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, the rDNA loci are located on the sex chromosomes (X and Y), each containing ~200–250 copies of rDNA (Figure 2A) (Ritossa et al., 1971).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The Y rDNA locus is always associated with the nucleolus when GSCs have typical nucleolar morphology, whereas the X rDNA locus was not, irrespective of age.
source: By combining DNA FISH with immunofluorescence staining to detect nucleoli, we found that the Y rDNA locus is always associated with the nucleolus when GSCs have typical nucleolar morphology, whereas the X rDNA locus was not, irrespective of age (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a primary finding from DNA FISH experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Y rDNA is actively transcribed in Drosophila male GSCs, whereas X rDNA is not.
source: Because the assembly of the nucleolus reflects rDNA transcription, these results suggest that Y rDNA is actively transcribed, whereas X rDNA is not.
evidence: This is inferred from the nucleolar association data.

claim: When the nucleolus is fragmented, the ectopic nucleolus was almost always closely located near the X rDNA locus, irrespective of age (n = 46/46, 100.0% in 0–1 day old flies, n = 46/47, 97.9% in 40 day old flies).
source: Interestingly, when the nucleolus is fragmented, the ectopic nucleolus (typically the smaller one) was almost always closely located near the X rDNA locus, irrespective of age (Figure 2C, n = 46/46, 100.0% in 0–1 day old flies, n = 46/47, 97.9% in 40 day old flies).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from DNA FISH experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: X rDNA was associated with deformed nucleoli.
source: X rDNA was also associated with deformed nucleoli (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an observation from DNA FISH experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Most GSCs only transcribed Y rRNA.
source: We found that most GSCs only transcribed Y rRNA (Figure 2E,F,H), demonstrating that nucleolar dominance indeed occurs in the male germline, as observed in male larval neuroblasts (Greil and Ahmad, 2012; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a primary finding from SNP in situ hybridization shown in Figures 2E, F, and H.

claim: Nucleolar dominance occurs in the Drosophila male germline.
source: We found that most GSCs only transcribed Y rRNA (Figure 2E,F,H), demonstrating that nucleolar dominance indeed occurs in the male germline, as observed in male larval neuroblasts (Greil and Ahmad, 2012; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a primary finding from SNP in situ hybridization with citation to prior work in other cell types.

claim: In all GSCs with fragmented nucleoli, one nucleolus showed a Y SNP signal, whereas the other showed an X SNP signal (n > 40).
source: In all GSCs with fragmented nucleoli, one nucleolus (typically the larger one) showed a Y SNP signal, whereas the other showed an X SNP signal, supporting the idea that nucleolar fragmentation is associated with transcriptional activation of the X rDNA locus (Figure 2E,G, n > 40).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from SNP in situ hybridization shown in Figures 2E and G.

claim: The number of GSCs expressing X rRNA increased from 18.2 ± 3.0% at 0 days old to 37.2 ± 2.4% at 40 days old.
source: As flies age, many GSCs exhibited expression of rRNA from both the Y and X chromosomes (Figure 2G,H). The number of GSCs expressing X rRNA increased from 18.2 ± 3.0% at 0 days old to 37.2 ± 2.4% at 40 days old (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from SNP in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Atypical nucleolar morphology that accumulates in GSCs during aging is due to activation of the normally silent X rDNA locus.
source: These results, together with the above result that showed association of the X rDNA locus with fragmented/deformed nucleoli (Figure 2A–F), strongly suggest that atypical nucleolar morphology that accumulates in GSCs during aging is due to activation of the normally silent X rDNA locus, causing rDNA transcription from two separate chromosomes, each forming distinct nucleoli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: There was a significant reduction in rDNA copy number in testes from old flies compared to young flies.
source: To address the possibility that rDNA copy number might be decreased during aging in male GSCs, we first isolated genomic DNA from testes of young and old flies and quantified their rDNA copy number using a previously published qPCR-based method for quantifying rDNA copy number (Supplementary file 2) (Aldrich and Maggert, 2014), and found a significant reduction in rDNA copy number (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from qPCR experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Copy number loss during aging was observed across all the mature rRNA genes in the 45S cistron (18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNA genes).
source: This copy number loss was observed across all the mature rRNA genes in the 45S cistron (18S, 5.8S and 28S rRNA genes).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from qPCR experiments.

claim: The copy number of R1 and R2 retrotransposable elements did not decrease with age.
source: Interestingly, the copy number of R1 and R2 retrotransposable elements did not decrease with age (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: R1 and R2 retrotransposable elements selectively insert into the 28S rRNA gene, and inserted rDNA units are transcriptionally repressed.
source: R1 and R2 retrotransposable elements selectively insert into the 28S rRNA gene, and inserted rDNA units are transcriptionally repressed (Ye and Eickbush, 2006).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: rDNA copy number loss primarily occurs in uninserted, actively-transcribed rDNA.
source: These results suggest that the rDNA copy number loss primarily occurs in uninserted, actively-transcribed rDNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that R1/R2-inserted copies are maintained while total rDNA decreases.

claim: Loss of rDNA copy number is associated with its transcriptional activity.
source: These results imply that loss of rDNA copy number is associated with its transcriptional activity, consistent with the well-established notion that collision between transcription and replication machineries causes rDNA instability (Helmrich et al., 2013; Takeuchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Y:X ratio of the 18S rRNA gene was 1.35 ± 0.31 and that of the 240 bp repeat intergenic spacer (240-IGS) was 2.88 ± 0.60 in wild type (yw) at day 0.
source: By using this method, we found that Y:X ratio of the 18S rRNA gene was 1.35 ± 0.31 and that of the 240 bp repeat intergenic spacer (240-IGS) was 2.88 ± 0.60 in wild type (yw) at day 0, indicating that Y chromosome harbors slightly more rDNA than X chromosome in the wild type strain (yw) used in this study.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DNA FISH experiments.

claim: Y chromosome harbors slightly more rDNA than X chromosome in the wild type strain (yw).
source: By using this method, we found that Y:X ratio of the 18S rRNA gene was 1.35 ± 0.31 and that of the 240 bp repeat intergenic spacer (240-IGS) was 2.88 ± 0.60 in wild type (yw) at day 0, indicating that Y chromosome harbors slightly more rDNA than X chromosome in the wild type strain (yw) used in this study.
evidence: This is inferred from the Y:X ratio measurements.

claim: The Y:X 18S rRNA gene ratio dropped from 1.35 ± 0.31 to 0.70 ± 0.25 by 40 days.
source: By using this method, we compared Y:X rDNA ratio in day 0 vs. day 40 old testes. We found that the Y:X 18S rRNA gene ratio dropped from 1.35 ± 0.31 to 0.70 ± 0.25 by 40 days (Figure 3E) and that the Y:X 240-IGS ratio reduced from 2.88 ± 0.60 at 0 days to 1.86 ± 0.58 by 40 days (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DNA FISH experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The Y:X 240-IGS ratio reduced from 2.88 ± 0.60 at 0 days to 1.86 ± 0.58 by 40 days.
source: By using this method, we compared Y:X rDNA ratio in day 0 vs. day 40 old testes. We found that the Y:X 18S rRNA gene ratio dropped from 1.35 ± 0.31 to 0.70 ± 0.25 by 40 days (Figure 3E) and that the Y:X 240-IGS ratio reduced from 2.88 ± 0.60 at 0 days to 1.86 ± 0.58 by 40 days (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DNA FISH experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The change in Y:X ratio during aging reflects Y rDNA loss, instead of X rDNA expansion.
source: Although the quantitative FISH method is only capable of detecting the ratio between X and Y, but not the absolute amount on each chromosome, the fact that overall germline rDNA copy number decreases during aging as demonstrated by qPCR (Figure 3A) suggests the change in Y:X ratio reflects Y rDNA loss, instead of X rDNA expansion.
evidence: This is inferred from combining qPCR and FISH data.

claim: GSCs in X/Df(YS)bb flies exhibited atypical nucleolar morphology at a frequency comparable to 40-day-old wild type flies even at a young age.
source: To directly address the causal relationship whether reduced rDNA copy number on the Y chromosome causes disrupted nucleolar morphology in GSCs, we examined GSC nucleolar morphology in X/Df(YS)bb flies, which harbors a partial deletion of Y rDNA. Even at a young age, GSCs in these flies exhibited atypical nucleolar morphology at a frequency comparable to 40-day-old wild type flies (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with Y rDNA deletion mutants shown in Figures 3G and H.

claim: Reduced rDNA copy number on the Y chromosome causes disrupted nucleolar morphology in GSCs.
source: To directly address the causal relationship whether reduced rDNA copy number on the Y chromosome causes disrupted nucleolar morphology in GSCs, we examined GSC nucleolar morphology in X/Df(YS)bb flies, which harbors a partial deletion of Y rDNA. Even at a young age, GSCs in these flies exhibited atypical nucleolar morphology at a frequency comparable to 40-day-old wild type flies (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: This causal relationship is supported by experiments with Y rDNA deletion mutants.

claim: qPCR on genomic DNA collected from testes of newly-eclosed F1 flies showed a significant reduction in the rDNA copy number when compared to young P0 flies (0d P0), but similar to 40 day old P0 (40d P0).
source: qPCR on genomic DNA collected from testes of newly-eclosed F1 flies showed a significant reduction in the rDNA copy number when compared to young P0 flies (0d P0), but similar to 40 day old P0 (40d P0) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from qPCR experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Old parents transmit reduced rDNA copy number to their offspring.
source: Again, the number of R1- and R2-inserted rDNA copies was not significantly affected. These results suggest that old parents transmit reduced rDNA copy number to their offspring.
evidence: This is concluded from the qPCR data on F1 progeny.

claim: Nucleolar morphology in F1 GSCs from old parents was perturbed, with only 59.1% of GSCs displaying typical nucleolar morphology in 0-day-old F1 sons (0d F1), similar to 40-day-old P0 fathers (40d P0).
source: Consistent with the reduced copy number of rDNA in F1 sons measured by qPCR, nucleolar morphology in F1 GSCs from old parents was also perturbed, with only 59.1% of GSCs displaying typical nucleolar morphology in 0-day-old F1 sons (0d F1), similar to 40-day-old P0 fathers (40d P0) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SNP in situ hybridization demonstrated similar levels of activation of the X rDNA locus in 40-day-old P0 and 0-day-old F1 GSCs from the sons of old fathers.
source: Furthermore, SNP in situ hybridization demonstrated similar levels of activation of the X rDNA locus in 40-day-old P0 and 0-day-old F1 GSCs from the sons of old fathers, consistent with disrupted Y rDNA copy number in these flies (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from SNP in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Male GSC nucleolar morphology is determined solely by the age of the inherited Y chromosome.
source: In contrast, when young fathers (contributing Yyoung) were crossed to 40 day old virgin mothers (contributing Xold), their offspring containing Xold and Yyoung chromosomes did not show perturbed nucleolar morphology (Figure 4F, column one vs. column 4), suggesting that male GSC nucleolar morphology is determined solely by the age of the inherited Y chromosome.
evidence: This is concluded from genetic crosses shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The state of the X chromosome (Xyoung vs. Xold) passed from the mother appears to affect the degree of disruption of nucleolar morphology in the context of the Y chromosome from the old father (Yold).
source: However, the state of the X chromosome (Xyoung vs. Xold) passed from the mother appears to affect the degree of disruption of nucleolar morphology in the context of the Y chromosome from the old father (Yold) (Figure 4F, column 2 and column 3).
evidence: This is observed from genetic crosses shown in Figure 4F.

claim: F1 sons from old fathers recovered nucleolar morphology as they age, specifically during the first 10 days after eclosion.
source: Although F1 sons from old fathers started with disrupted GSC nucleolar morphology, we unexpectedly found that nucleolar morphology recovered as these F1 sons age (Figure 5A). Interestingly, the recovery was specifically observed during the first 10 days after eclosion.
evidence: This is a primary finding shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At 10 days, F1 sons from old fathers recovered to the point where they were comparable to F1 sons of the same age from young fathers.
source: At 10 days, F1 sons from old fathers recovered to the point where they were comparable to F1 sons of the same age from young fathers, after which nucleolar morphology in these two populations worsened at a similar rate (Figure 5A, compare to Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing nucleolar morphology data in Figures 5A and 1D.

claim: X rDNA expression in F1 sons from old fathers diminished until 10 days, after which it again increased.
source: Concomitant with the recovery of nucleolar morphology, X rDNA expression in F1 sons from old fathers diminished until 10 days, after which it again increased (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from SNP in situ hybridization shown in Figures 5B and C.

claim: Y:X rDNA ratio recovered during the recovery period in germ cells.
source: During this period, Y: X rDNA ratio also recovered (Figure 5D), revealing remarkable ability of the Y chromosome rDNA to expand in copy number.
evidence: This is a finding from DNA FISH experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Y chromosome rDNA has remarkable ability to expand in copy number.
source: During this period, Y: X rDNA ratio also recovered (Figure 5D), revealing remarkable ability of the Y chromosome rDNA to expand in copy number.
evidence: This is inferred from the recovery of Y:X ratio shown in Figure 5D.

claim: rDNA expansion may be a stochastic event that occurs in individual GSCs.
source: Interestingly, while we found many germ cells to have recovered Y:X rDNA ratio, there was also a large number of germ cells that apparently did not recover (Figure 5D), suggesting that rDNA expansion may be a stochastic event that occurs in individual GSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the heterogeneity in Y:X ratios shown in Figure 5D.

claim: mus-101 and mei-41 mutants failed to recover typical nucleolar morphology in the GSCs of animals that inherited their Y chromosome from aged fathers.
source: Indeed, we found that mus-101 and mei-41 mutants failed to recover typical nucleolar morphology in the GSCs of animals that inherited their Y chromosome from aged fathers (Figure 6A–C, compare to Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with mutants shown in Figures 6A-C.

claim: Mutations in mus-102, which is required for DNA damage repair but not for rDNA magnification, had no effect on the recovery of GSC nucleolar morphology.
source: Conversely, mutations in mus-102, which is required for DNA damage repair but not for rDNA magnification (Hawley and Tartof, 1985), had no effect on the recovery of GSC nucleolar morphology (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with mus-102 mutants shown in Figure 6D, with citation to prior work.

claim: Similar mechanisms underlie rDNA magnification and rDNA recovery in young sons from old fathers.
source: These results indicate that similar mechanisms might underlie these two phenomena, and that rDNA magnification may be the manifestation of the mechanisms that normally maintains rDNA copy number.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic requirements for both processes.

claim: rDNA magnification may be the manifestation of the mechanisms that normally maintains rDNA copy number.
source: These results indicate that similar mechanisms might underlie these two phenomena, and that rDNA magnification may be the manifestation of the mechanisms that normally maintains rDNA copy number.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic requirements for both processes.

claim: There was a significant difference in GSC nucleolar morphology between the sons of 40-day-old yw and mus-101D1 mutant (p=0.0070).
source: However, there was a significant difference between the sons of 40-day-old yw and mus-101D1mutant (Figure 7B, p=0.0070), suggesting that the mus-101 mutant fathers suffer more Y chromosome rDNA loss during aging compared to the yw fathers.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: mus-101 mutant fathers suffer more Y chromosome rDNA loss during aging compared to the yw fathers.
source: However, there was a significant difference between the sons of 40-day-old yw and mus-101D1mutant (Figure 7B, p=0.0070), suggesting that the mus-101 mutant fathers suffer more Y chromosome rDNA loss during aging compared to the yw fathers.
evidence: This is inferred from the nucleolar morphology data in Figure 7B.

claim: The same molecular machineries underlie normal germline rDNA maintenance and the phenomenon of rDNA magnification.
source: This result suggests that the same molecular machineries might underlie normal germline rDNA maintenance and the phenomenon of rDNA magnification.
evidence: This is inferred from the requirement of mus-101 for both processes.

claim: Nucleolar dominance is a phenomenon originally discovered in interspecific hybrids, wherein entire rDNA loci from one species are predominantly activated and those from the other species are silenced.
source: Nucleolar dominance is a phenomenon originally discovered in interspecific hybrids, wherein entire rDNA loci from one species are predominantly activated and those from the other species are silenced (Chen et al., 1998; Chen and Pikaard, 1997; Durica and Krider, 1977; Preuss and Pikaard, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Nucleolar dominance occurs within D. melanogaster males, where Y chromosome rDNA is predominantly expressed, whereas X rDNA is silent.
source: However, it was shown that nucleolar dominance also occurs within the D. melanogaster males, where Y chromosome rDNA is predominantly expressed, whereas X rDNA is silent (Greil and Ahmad, 2012; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: By limiting the transcription of rDNA to one chromosome (Y chromosome), cells can reduce the risk of deleterious recombination events between the X and Y chromosomes.
source: There are a few potential explanations why this might be advantageous: (1) by limiting the transcription of rDNA (thus potential DNA breaks) to one chromosome (i.e. Y chromosome), cells can reduce the risk of deleterious recombination events between the X and Y chromosomes, (2) by maintaining a stable chromosomal locus (X rDNA) for later use, stem cells might be able to extend their life span, delaying the timing of collapse and thus the overall aging.
evidence: This is proposed as a potential explanation for nucleolar dominance.

claim: By maintaining a stable chromosomal locus (X rDNA) for later use, stem cells might be able to extend their life span, delaying the timing of collapse and thus the overall aging.
source: There are a few potential explanations why this might be advantageous: (1) by limiting the transcription of rDNA (thus potential DNA breaks) to one chromosome (i.e. Y chromosome), cells can reduce the risk of deleterious recombination events between the X and Y chromosomes, (2) by maintaining a stable chromosomal locus (X rDNA) for later use, stem cells might be able to extend their life span, delaying the timing of collapse and thus the overall aging.
evidence: This is proposed as a potential explanation for nucleolar dominance.

claim: Cells evolved nucleolar dominance to protect their rDNA loci from deleterious recombination.
source: It is tempting to speculate that cells evolved nucleolar dominance to protect their rDNA loci, which are distributed among multiple chromosomes, from deleterious recombination.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Female neuroblasts exhibit co-dominance between two X chromosome rDNA loci.
source: It was reported that female neuroblasts exhibit co-dominance between two X chromosome rDNA loci (Greil and Ahmad, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: rDNA copy number changes in response to nutrient conditions, and such copy number changes are inherited to the next generations.
source: It has been shown that rDNA copy number changes in response to nutrient conditions, and such copy number changes are inherited to the next generations (Aldrich and Maggert, 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: Tandem rDNA repeats are unstable in Drosophila male GSCs, similar to their well characterized instability in yeast.
source: Our findings reveal that tandem rDNA repeats are unstable in Drosophila male GSCs, similar to their well characterized instability in yeast, suggesting rDNA loss may occur in other metazoan stem cell populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: rDNA loss may occur in other metazoan stem cell populations.
source: Our findings reveal that tandem rDNA repeats are unstable in Drosophila male GSCs, similar to their well characterized instability in yeast, suggesting rDNA loss may occur in other metazoan stem cell populations.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings in Drosophila GSCs.

claim: The germline of young animals has the capacity to restore lost rDNA copies.
source: Although this instability in germ cells can cause the inheritance of reduced rDNA copies, the germline of young animals has the capacity to restore the lost rDNA copies.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings on rDNA recovery.

claim: The dynamic contraction and expansion of rDNA loci across generations normally maintains sufficient rDNA copies throughout a population.
source: These findings suggest that the dynamic contraction and expansion of rDNA loci across generations normally maintains sufficient rDNA copies throughout a population.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: In mouse hematopoietic stem cells, replicative stress is a major driver of stem cell aging.
source: It was shown that in mouse hematopoietic stem cells, replicative stress is a major driver of stem cell aging (Flach et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.

claim: In mouse hematopoietic stem cells, signs of replication stress (accumulation of γ-H2Ax) are observed mainly in the nucleolus.
source: Curiously, they observed signs of replication stress (accumulation of γ-H2Ax) mainly in the nucleolus, but it remained unclear why the nucleolus specifically accumulates replication stress.
evidence: This is stated with reference to prior work.

claim: Destabilization of rDNA loci may underlie age-associated accumulation of replication stress in the nucleolus.
source: We speculate that destabilization of rDNA loci may underlie age-associated accumulation of replication stress in the nucleolus.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Cells with fewer rDNA copies will have a larger proportion of their rDNA being transcribed than cells with more copies.
source: This constant requirement for rDNA transcription means that those cells with fewer rDNA copies will have a larger proportion of their rDNA being transcribed than cells with more copies, as has been shown in yeast.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence with reference to yeast studies.

claim: Increased collisions between replication and transcription machineries has been observed in a yeast strain with reduced rDNA copy number, leading to replication stress.
source: Increased collisions between replication and transcription machineries has been observed in a yeast strain with reduced rDNA copy number, leading to replication stress (Takeuchi et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work.
